content:
A common claim holds that people come to Islam by birth, by marriage or by pressure, and never by thinking. The figures say otherwise. Among American converts to Islam, Pew Research Center found that 19% had been religiously unaffiliated before they converted, and the reason given most often was a preference for Islam's beliefs and teachings.[1]

People who reach Islam from unbelief or doubt meet the same questions on the way: why anything exists, why God is one, why there is suffering, where morality comes from, and whether a book can be from God. Michael David Shapiro, who wrote of his own path, put his starting point in plain words: "My belief in God was uncertain."[2]

This article aims to provide context to those questions, insha'Allah, in five questions and the answers the Quran gives them. The Quran invites the inquiry itself: "Do they not then earnestly seek to understand the Qur'an, or are their hearts locked up by them?" (47:24).[3]

The first question is why there is something and not nothing. The Quran puts it as a choice: "Were they created of nothing, or were they themselves the creators? Or did they create the heavens and the earth? Nay, they have no firm belief" (52:35 to 36).[3]

Shapiro weighed the same choice. "I analyzed both atheist and theist beliefs," he wrote, and the line that turned him was "Every design has a designer."[2]

The atheist reply is that the universe may simply be a brute fact. The Quranic question is whether the reader holds that answer with "firm belief", or holds it because the other answer is unwelcome. We set out the argument in full in 5 reasons why the universe demands a creator.

Belief in a creator does not yet answer how many. The Quran answers from order: "If there were, in the heavens and the earth, other gods besides Allah, there would have been confusion in both!" (21:22).[3] The theologians called this the argument from mutual hindrance, burhān al-tamānuʿ: two wills that could each prevail cannot both be supreme.

Shapiro reached the same point in his own words: "I figured only one; knowing that a divided God is weaker than One God."[2] Surah al-Ikhlas gives the doctrine in four verses: "Say: He is Allah, the One and Only; Allah, the Eternal, Absolute; He begetteth not, nor is He begotten; And there is none like unto Him" (112:1 to 4).[3]

Suffering is the objection most often given for unbelief. The Quran does not promise a world without it. It names the purpose of life and death as a test: "He Who created Death and Life, that He may try which of you is best in deed" (67:2).[3]

It names the losses too, and the response it asks for: "Be sure we shall test you with something of fear and hunger, some loss in goods or lives or the fruits (of your toil), but give glad tidings to those who patiently persevere, Who say, when afflicted with calamity: 'To Allah We belong, and to Him is our return'" (2:155 to 156).[3] The account of Moses and the servant of God in Surah al-Kahf shows events whose meaning lies beyond what a witness can see (18:60 to 82).

These verses give a framework, and they do not explain every grief. No Muslim answer to the question should be used to dismiss another person's pain. We set out six answers from the sources in why does God allow suffering?

Atheists can be honest, just and kind, and many are. The question is what makes an obligation binding, beyond preference or agreement. The Quran grounds it in accountability before God: "Then shall anyone who has done an atom's weight of good, see it! And anyone who has done an atom's weight of evil, shall see it" (99:7 to 8).[3]

Shapiro put the point bluntly while he was still weighing religions: "If I don't have fear of strict punishment, then why should I be moral?"[2] The Quran's standard of justice reaches the self and the family: "stand out firmly for justice, as witnesses to Allah, even as against yourselves, or your parents, or your kin" (4:135).[3] We set out the case against secular grounding in why morality is impossible without God.

Arguments for a creator do not prove a scripture. That question needs the scripture itself, and the Quran asks to be read and tested: "Behold! in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day,- there are indeed Signs for men of understanding" (3:190).[3]

Scholars of conversion have studied what reading means to converts. Iulian Vamanu and Elysia Guzik examine the meanings of reading in recent conversion narratives in Christianity and Islam.[4] A reader's experience persuades the reader; the transmission of the text, its claims and its history are tested separately, and the Quran stakes its case on that test.

The bottom line

Conversion from unbelief to Islam runs through five questions: existence, the oneness of God, suffering, morality and revelation. The Quran answers each in its own words, and asks to be examined. A convert's story shows why one person found the answers convincing; it proves nothing on its own, since people also leave faith.

The argument has to stand on its evidence, and the choice belongs to the person: "Let there be no compulsion in religion: Truth stands out clear from Error" (2:256).[3] We set out what a single testimony can and cannot show in what can a former Muslim's testimony show about Islam? Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Pew Research Center, "U.S. Muslims Concerned About Their Place in Society, but Continue to Believe in the American Dream", chapter 6, "Religious Beliefs and Practices", 26 July 2017.
  2. Michael David Shapiro, "Michael David Shapiro, Ex-Jew, Russia", IslamReligion.com, 5 May 2008; republished as "A Jew's Journey to Islam", Arab News, 2 September 2016.
  3. Quran 2:155 to 156; 2:256; 3:190; 4:135; 18:60 to 82; 21:22; 47:24; 52:35 to 36; 67:2; 99:7 to 8; 112:1 to 4, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  4. Iulian Vamanu and Elysia Guzik, "'Closer to God': Meanings of Reading in Recent Conversion Narratives within Christianity and Islam", Journal of Religious & Theological Information 14, nos. 3–4 (2015), pp. 63–78.
